Neighbourhood of form is not identity of case.

**Matthew 4:4–10 / Luke 4:4–12.** “It is written” and “it is written again” judge a use of Scripture by Scripture. The practice of wording-as-force is already Chapter 48. The present file is not a second wilderness-trial.

**Luke 24:44–47.** He opens what was written in the law, the prophets, and the psalms concerning Himself. Confirmation of received Scripture as a whole remains Chapter 48. The present file is one controversy’s logic.

These neighbours establish that reasoning from the Graphē is His practice, not an isolated trick in John 10. They do not establish that John 10 is already those other arguments, or that a catalogue of “it is written” has performed this chapter’s a fortiori. Shared practice with a new function is not duplication. A new function treated as a catalogue would be duplication.

Thus:

> **Neighbouring “it is written” arguments illuminate that He reasons from wording as court. They are not this blasphemy-trial, not this psalm, and not a substitute for reconstructing John 10:35–36.**

---

# 61.31 After the Reasoning, the Return to Works

John 10:37–38 returns to works after the Scripture-argument. Chapter 59 located that return as remainder-context. This chapter needs one logical observation, not a retry of Chapter 45.

The Scripture-argument and the works-argument are not rivals in the discourse. They are two courts the discourse actually uses. Works bear witness. Writing tries the charge. After the writing has tried the charge, works are offered again: if He does not the works of the Father, believe Him not; if He does, believe the works, that they may know and believe that the Father is in Him and He in the Father.

The return prevents a misreading of this chapter as a claim that He reasons from Scripture instead of from works. He reasons from Scripture in verses 34–36. He does not thereby discard works. The weight assigned to the written text is not a denial of other witness. It is the assignment of court-place to the Graphē in the blasphemy-trial.

They seek again to take Him (John 10:39). The argument did not compel consent. Compelled consent is not the test of validity. Validity is whether the inference follows. It follows. Refusal follows also, as the record states. The record’s honesty about refusal is part of the evidence that the scene is not a constructed victory-tale in which opponents vanish. It is a controversy.

Thus:

> **The return to works after the Scripture-argument shows two witnesses in one discourse, not a rivalry. Weight assigned to the Graphē is not a denial of works. Refusal after the argument is not a defeat of the inference.**

---

# 61.32 Distinctions Required by the Conclusion

The conclusion requires three distinctions to be kept in force together. They have been drawn; they must now be named as the conclusion’s own shape.

**Exhibiting the logic is not the finished lexical and doctrinal treatment of “cannot be broken.”** The clause functions. Chapters 62–63 remain. Function is not the later why.

**This chapter is not Chapter 65.** Court in this dispute is not the finished claim that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived.

**Reasoning from Scripture is not Christ-level authority for every later interpreter.** The reader may and must reason through the Word. The reader does not become this Speaker by doing so.

These distinctions are not stacked hedges. They are the doctrine’s edges. A conclusion without edges would steal later files or transfer authority. A conclusion with only edges and no warrant would be the stacked hedge the methodology forbids. The warrant has been stated. The edges belong to it.

Thus:

> **The conclusion’s required distinctions are three: logic exhibited is not unbreakability finished; this file is not the Graphē-gate; His reasoning is not every later interpreter’s authority. Edges are the shape of the doctrine, not delayed doubt.**

---

# 61.33 What the Reasoning Explicitly Establishes

The record is explicit on the following, and this chapter claims them as explicit.

- He asks whether it is written in their law, “I said, Ye are gods” (John 10:34).
- He treats that wording as a calling of those to whom the word of God came (John 10:35a).
- He states, in the same sentence, that the scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35b).
- He applies the case to the charge against Him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, because He said “I am the Son of God” (John 10:36).
- The application is put as a question that returns their word “blasphemest.”
- The cited wording is the wording of Psalm 82:6, whose addressees are those who judge under God (Chapters 59–60 used, not retried).

Those are not inferences from a later logic-textbook. They are the unit plus the already-established citation.

Thus:

> **What is explicit is the written calling, the characterization, the standing-clause as His assertion, the sanctified-and-sent identification, the Son-claim as the prosecuted speech, and the returned charge as a question.**

---

# 61.34 What This Chapter Does Not Yet Establish

The same honesty requires a list of what this chapter does not claim to have finished, not as doubt about the reasoning, but as the shape of the movement.

- It has not defined “broken,” nor answered why the scripture cannot be broken from what Scripture is (Chapters 62–63).
- It has not examined John 17:17, “thy word is truth,” as Graphē-doctrine (Chapter 64).
- It has not concluded that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived (Chapter 65).
- It has not written Movement IX’s mishandling-files, nor Movement X’s labour-files, nor the Six First Principles.
- It has not transferred Christ-level authority to later interpreters.
- It has not reduced the Son-claim to the judges’ title, and it has not written a completed Christology from this inference alone.

The list is sequence. Sequence is not a second conclusion that the reasoning-file is weak.

Thus:

> **The reasoning does not consume the later files. The later files do not postpone the reasoning. Each question remains its own question.**

---

# 61.35 Competing Claim: The Argument as Mere Wordplay

The first live reduction is to treat John 10:34–36 as a pun on θεοί / θεόν.

The reduction says: He noticed a vocabulary-overlap; He exploited it to embarrass opponents; there is no lesser and greater case; there is no court; there is only a sound.

The reduction fails for reasons already in the unit.

A pun does not require “unto whom the word of God came.” Characterization is case, not sound.

A pun does not require “the scripture cannot be broken” as a parenthetical of force. Standing is court, not wit.

A pun does not require “whom the Father hath sanctified, and sent into the world” as the identification of the subject. Greater commission is comparison, not a punchline.

A pun does not return a capital charge as a question under “your law.” Blasphemy-trial is not a joke.

Wordplay, as a charge against the argument, is itself a refusal to follow the joints. The joints are condition, characterization, standing, application. Followed as joints, they are logic. Ignored as joints, they can be called a pun by anyone who wishes not to be tried by the writing.

Seriousness about the word “gods” is required because He cites it. Seriousness that discards the case, the standing, and the application is not seriousness about the argument. It is capture by a sound.

Thus:

> **Treating the argument as mere wordplay fails. The unit is a written case, asserted as standing Scripture, applied to a capital charge against the sanctified and sent Son. A pun does not have those joints.**

---

# 61.36 Competing Claim: Ignoring the A Fortiori

The second live reduction is to treat verses 34–36 as citation plus restated identity, with no comparison of lesser and greater.

The reduction says: He quotes a psalm; He then says He is the Son of God; the middle is ornamental; there is no “if… then how much more.”

The reduction fails because verse 36 is not a new start. It is the apodosis-force of verse 35’s condition, put as a question. “If he called them gods… Say ye of him… Thou blasphemest…?” is one argument. A restated identity would not need the “if.” A citation-plus-shout would not need “unto whom the word of God came.”

The reduction also fails because it cannot explain the sanctified-and-sent identification as greater-commission language. If there is no comparison, “sanctified and sent” is colour. In the argument it is the greater case. Colour-readings are the same family as decoration-readings. They fail the same test: remove the member and see whether the argument remains. Remove the comparison, and the writing no longer tries the charge. It only sits beside it.

Ignoring the a fortiori is often a pious-sounding move: one wishes to honour the Son-claim by not “reducing” it to an inference. The honour is misplaced. He is the One who infers. To refuse His inference in order to protect His claim is to protect a claim He did not make in this form. He made the claim as the greater case of a written argument. Following Him includes following that form.

The reconstruction remains honest that “how much more” is not an adverb in the verse. Ignoring the a fortiori on that ground would confuse explicit wording with warranted structure. Structure is in the verses. The tag is later. The tag may be dropped. The structure may not.

Thus:

> **Ignoring the a fortiori fails. Verse 36 is the application of verse 35’s written case to a greater subject. Citation plus restated identity is not the argument He gave.**

---

# 61.37 Competing Claim: This Chapter as Already Chapters 62–65

The third live reduction is architectural collapse.

The reduction says: once the logic has been followed, unbreakability is finished, “thy word is truth” is finished, and the Graphē-gate is finished.

The reduction fails because those are different questions.

Chapters 62–63 ask what “broken” means and why the scripture cannot be broken from what Scripture is. This chapter has used the clause as force in the chain. Force in the chain is not the dedicated sense and not the dedicated why.

Chapter 64 asks how God’s Word is truth. This chapter has not examined John 17:17.

Chapter 65 asks why the Graphē is the primary written authority. This chapter has shown that in this dispute He treats the Graphē as court and settling-material. Court in this dispute is not the finished gate.

Collapse would make Movement VIII a single file with six titles. The locked TOC forbids that. Sequence is the remedy for collapse, not a slight upon the reasoning.

Thus:

> **This chapter is not already Chapters 62–65. Exhibiting the logic and the weight is not unbreakability, not John 17:17, and not the Graphē-gate.**

---

# 61.38 Competing Claim: Reducing the Son-Claim to the Judges' Title

The fourth live reduction is identity in the opposite direction from collapse: not inflating this file into later files, but deflating the greater case into the lesser.

The reduction says: Jesus claims only to be a god in the sense of Psalm 82’s judges; the argument is a plea for that classification; oneness with the Father is thereby removed.

The reduction fails because the argument is a fortiori, not identity, as already shown. It fails also because the prosecuted speech is “I am the Son of God” in a discourse that has already said “I and my Father are one,” and because verse 36 identifies Him by the Father’s sanctifying and sending, not by the psalm’s indictment of a failed bench.

The reduction often presents itself as sober exegesis: do not over-read. Sober exegesis is required. Sober exegesis reads the comparison as comparison. Under-reading the greater case is not sobriety. It is the refusal of verse 36’s identification.

This chapter’s own limit remains in force: the a fortiori defends the Son-claim as not blasphemy under their law; it does not, by itself, write every later Christological file. Chapters 44–45 remain the claims-and-works files. The present refusal is of a different error: the error of using the lesser case to erase the greater. Defense of a claim is not the erasure of the claim.

Thus:

> **Reducing the Son-claim to the judges’ title fails. The lesser naming is precedent, not identity. He is the Father’s sanctified and sent Son, arguing from a written lesser case, not pleading to be only that case.**

---

# 61.39 Reason Through the Evidence

The inference can now be exhibited as a whole.

**Premise 1.** John 10:34–36 is Christ’s appeal to what is written as decisive in a blasphemy-dispute; the cited wording is “I said, Ye are gods”; those so called are those to whom the word of God came; the unit contains “the scripture cannot be broken” and applies the case to the sanctified and sent Son (Chapter 59).

**Premise 2.** That wording is Psalm 82:6 in a judicial psalm addressing those who judge under God; He uses the written wording because the case requires the words as Holy Writ already in force (Chapter 60).

**Premise 3.** Verse 35’s “if” takes that written calling as admitted premise, not as doubt and not as flourish.

**Premise 4.** The lesser case is real, written, and lesser: commissioned hearers named “gods,” not the Most High, mortal, not the unique sent One.

**Premise 5.** The greater case is He whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, who has said “I am the Son of God,” the subject of their blasphemy-charge.

**Premise 6.** The standing-clause treats the lesser naming as not to be set aside. Its dedicated why remains later; its function as force in the chain is used here.

**Premise 7.** A fortiori is the structure verse 36 forces: if even the lesser written naming stands, the charge against the greater does not stand as a mere inference from God-vocabulary used of a man. The comparison is greater, not identical; related vocabulary is not equivocation.

**Premise 8.** He is the Truth who also offers works; He nevertheless argues from their law first in this answer. That order is the assignment of court-weight to the Graphē in the dispute.

**Inference.** Therefore He reasons from what is written as the court of the dispute, assigning the written text the weight of settling-material for the charge’s terms; the logic is the a fortiori from Psalm 82’s standing naming to the sanctified and sent Son’s claim; competing reductions — wordplay, ignored comparison, collapse into Chapters 62–65, identity with the judges — fail as accounts of the unit.

The inference is not a deduction from a later creed. It is the unit plus the already-established citation plus the already-established standing of the writing as their law. Alternative global explanations fail as accounts of the conjunction, as already shown.

Thus:

> **The warranted inference is that John 10:35–36 is Christ’s a fortiori from the written lesser naming to the greater Son-claim, with the Graphē as court and settling-material, not as decoration.**

---

# 61.40 Explicit Versus Inferred

Honesty about the inference requires a clean line.

**Explicit.** The sentences of John 10:33–36. The citation of “I said, Ye are gods.” The characterization “unto whom the word of God came.” The clause “the scripture cannot be broken.” The identification “whom the Father hath sanctified, and sent into the world.” The because-clause “I am the Son of God.” The returned charge “Thou blasphemest.” The psalm’s judicial argument as already established.

**Inferred, as warranted.** That verse 35’s “if” is admitted premise. That the form is a fortiori from lesser to greater, even without πόσῳ μᾶλλον in the verse. That the Graphē occupies the place of court rather than decoration. That the weight assigned is settling-material for the charge’s terms. That the two cases are not identical. That “gods” and “Son of God” are related without equivocation. That later interpreter-reasoning is not thereby given His authority.

**Not inferred here.** The definition of “broken.” The why of unbreakability from what Scripture is. John 17:17 as Graphē-doctrine. The Graphē-gate. A completed Christology from this inference alone. A reconstructed academy or named school as the argument’s source. Unverifiable details of a scroll in the porch.

The line is the difference between a reasoning-file and a later-file. Crossing it would be theft. Refusing to infer what the conjunction warrants would be under-claim. The chapter has inferred what the conjunction warrants. It has not inferred what later premises must still supply.

Thus:

> **What is explicit has been distinguished from what is inferred. Later doctrines have not been inferred here. The warranted inferences about a fortiori, court-weight, and non-identity have been drawn.**

---

# 61.41 The Warranted Conclusion Stated with Full Force

The conclusion may now be stated without a remaining apology.

> **Christ reasons from what is written. John 10:35–36 is not a pun, not a restated shout beside a psalm, and not a plea to be classified only with Psalm 82’s judges. It is an a fortiori from a standing written naming. If the writing calls those to whom the word of God came “gods,” and the scripture cannot be broken, then the charge “Thou blasphemest,” spoken of Him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world because He said “I am the Son of God,” is a charge their law will not sustain as a mere inference from God-vocabulary used of a man. He treats the Graphē as the court of the dispute, not as decoration. He assigns the written text the weight of settling-material for the charge’s terms: their own law, as writing, as case, as standing, applied to a capital indictment. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving this as Christ’s reasoning from what is written, steps 5–6 of the locked John 10 arc. This is not yet the finished sense or why of “cannot be broken.” It is not yet John 17:17. It is not yet the Graphē-gate. It is not a grant of Christ-level authority to every later interpreter. It is the logic of the argument and the weight of the written text. That is this chapter’s conclusion.**

The remaining questions follow by sequence. The reasoning is already in force.

---

# 61.42 The Scope of This Stage

The scope of this stage is the logic of Christ’s argument and the weight He assigns to the written text.

It includes the definitions of reasoning-from-writing, logic, weight, and a fortiori; the control of the connectives; the use of “cannot be broken” as force in the chain; the lesser and greater cases; the reconstruction of the inference; the Graphē as court; the positive warrant; the refusal of wordplay, ignored comparison, architectural collapse, and identity-reduction; and the distinction between His reasoning and later interpreters’ authority.

It excludes the finished sense and why of “cannot be broken,” John 17:17, the Graphē-gate, and later mishandling and labour.

The scope is not a delay. It is the assignment. An assignment performed with full force is not a partial assignment. It is this assignment, complete.

Thus:

> **This stage is complete as the reasoning-file. Completeness of this stage is not completeness of Movement VIII.**

---

# 61.43 Apply the Standard

The governing standard of the book remains:

> **Do not merely tell the reader what to conclude. Give the reader the definitions, evidence, biblical record, reasoning, distinctions, and inferential steps necessary to see why the conclusion follows.**

And:

> **Do not make the reader choose between reason and Scripture. Teach the reader to reason through Scripture.**

This chapter has defined reasoning from what is written, the logic of the argument, the weight assigned to the text, and a fortiori. It has distinguished those objects from unbreakability finished, from the Graphē-gate, from Chapter 59’s scene, from Chapter 60’s psalm, from identity of cases, from wordplay, and from later interpreter-authority. It has used premises already in force and refused premises that remain later. It has followed the “if,” the lesser naming, the greater commission, the compared speech, and the returned charge. It has reconstructed the inference. It has stated the positive warrant. It has refused the live reductions. It has distinguished the explicit from the inferred.

The four governing questions have not been conflated. The ontological question — what stands as the court in this reasoning — has been answered as the received written Scripture. The epistemological question — how the charge is to be known as sustainable or not — has been answered by inference from that writing’s lesser case. The evidential question — what warrants treating this as His reasoning from the Graphē with court-weight — has been answered by the conjunction of order, their law, case, standing-clause as force, and application. The hermeneutical question of later mishandling remains later. The present file has not pretended to be Movement IX.

The Easton test has been applied in its proper analogue. A later writer may say that John 10 is a proof-text, or only a pun about gods, or already the whole doctrine of unbreakable Scripture, or already the Graphē-gate, or only a claim to be a judge. The manuscript has not accepted those sentences as premises. It has asked what the argument itself presents and what the record actually warrants.

Circularity has been refused. The argument is not: the Bible is authoritative because the Bible says it is authoritative; therefore this scene finishes the book. The argument is: this Person, already identified, in this controversy, reasons from this writing as court with this a fortiori; therefore the verdict on the Graphē continues here as logic and weight.

Prematurity has been refused. The chapter has not consumed “cannot be broken,” John 17:17, or the Graphē-gate.

Duplication has been refused. Scene remains Chapter 59. Psalm remains Chapter 60. Works remain Chapter 45. Confirmation remains Chapter 48. The present function is the dedicated logic and weight.

Thus:

> **The standard has been applied: the reasoning has been followed as Scripture’s own argument, not announced as a slogan, and not postponed as if the a fortiori were weak.**

---

# 61.44 From the Reasoning to “The Scripture Cannot Be Broken”

A reasoning, now followed as an a fortiori from standing writing, still leaves a further question.

The reasoning-file is in force. He has argued from “I said, Ye are gods.” The lesser case has been used as lesser. The greater case has been used as greater. The Graphē has been shown as court, not decoration. The weight assigned to the written text has been shown as settling-material for the charge’s terms. Those sentences are the cleared ground. They are not yet the dedicated examination of the clause that gave the lesser case its non-negotiable standing: “the scripture cannot be broken.”

If the logic were not followed, the next question would still be how He reasons. The logic has been followed. If this chapter were already that later examination of “broken,” the next file would be repetition. This chapter is not that later examination. The next question is therefore the construction the locked assignment names: the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken,” and what “broken” means in its argumentative context.

That is the proper open of the next chapter. Christ’s reasoning from what is written was never meant to be a pun about gods, and it was never meant to finish Movement VIII at the third step. It was meant to be the logic and the weight, sufficient to justify taking the next question, which is the question a standing-clause itself forces once it has been used as force: what does it mean that the scripture cannot be broken?

---

# What Has Been Established

This chapter has established:

1. **Christ’s reasoning from what is written, in this argument, is the movement from Graphē-premises to the present charge, not a new oracle, not a pun, and not the whole of Movement VIII.**
2. **The logic of the argument is condition, characterization, standing, and application — verses 35–36 as inference, not as a heap of clauses.**
3. **Weight assigned to the written text is the force of court and settling-material in this dispute, not decoration, not the finished why, and not the Graphē-gate.**
4. **A fortiori is from the written lesser naming of those who received God’s word as “gods” to the greater claim of the sanctified and sent Son. The form is reconstructed from the structure, not quoted as πόσῳ μᾶλλον.**
5. **The connectives of the unit are controlled as the argument’s joints, not as a later system’s substitutes.**
6. **“The scripture cannot be broken” functions here as asserted standing in the chain. Function is not Chapters 62–63.**
7. **The unit is recalled as a chain of inference, not retried as a Dedication-scene.**
8. **Verse 35’s “if” is admitted premise from their law, not doubt and not flourish.**
9. **The lesser case is those to whom the word of God came: real, written, and lesser than the Son.**
10. **“He called them gods” treats the wording as a naming that collides with a coarse blasphemy-standard.**
11. **The greater case is He whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.**
12. **The compared speech is “I am the Son of God,” related to the written naming without being reduced to it.**
13. **“Say ye… Thou blasphemest” is the conclusion-form: their charge returned under their law.**
14. **The a fortiori, reconstructed, is: if the lesser standing naming is not blasphemy, the greater Son-claim is not blasphemy merely as God-vocabulary used of a man.**
15. **The comparison is greater, not identical. He is not pleading to be one more judge.**
16. **The specified respect of the greater is commission: sanctified and sent into the world, greater than word-coming to the psalm’s bench.**
17. **“Gods” and “Son of God” are related vocabulary without equivocation.**
18. **The direction of inference is from writing to charge, not from charge to decorative verse.**
19. **The Graphē is the court, not decoration. He reasons from their law even as the Truth who also offers works.**
20. **The written text is settling-material for the charge’s terms.**
21. **Positive warrant for that weight is the argument’s order, their law, the case, the standing-clause as force, and the application.**
22. **Their own law is the unrecusable court of the a fortiori.**
23. **His reasoning does not confer Christ-level authority on every later interpreter.**
24. **Neighbouring Scripture-arguments illuminate practice and do not absorb this file.**
25. **The return to works shows two witnesses in one discourse, not a rivalry. Refusal after the argument is not defeat of the inference.**
26. **The conclusion’s required distinctions are three: logic ≠ finished unbreakability; this file ≠ Chapter 65; His reasoning ≠ every later interpreter’s authority.**
27. **What is explicit has been distinguished from what is inferred, and later doctrines have not been inferred here.**
28. **Treating the argument as mere wordplay fails.**
29. **Ignoring the a fortiori fails.**
30. **Treating this chapter as already Chapters 62–65 fails.**
31. **Reducing the Son-claim to the judges’ title fails.**
32. **This chapter continues Movement VIII because its assigned word has been stated.**
33. **This chapter opens Chapter 62 by naming the next necessary question without answering it.**
34. **What is reserved is Chapters 62–63 in full; Chapter 64 in full; Chapter 65 in full; Movements IX–X; First Principles; and σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*).**

---

# Chapter Summary

> **The chapter’s central conclusion:** John 10:35–36, read as the dedicated reasoning of the argument located in Chapter 59 and supplied with its exhibit in Chapter 60, is Christ’s a fortiori from what is written. If the writing calls those to whom the word of God came “gods,” and the scripture cannot be broken, the charge of blasphemy against the One the Father sanctified and sent, because He said “I am the Son of God,” is a charge their law will not sustain as a mere inference from God-vocabulary used of a man. He treats the Graphē as the court, not as decoration, and assigns the written text the weight of settling-material in the dispute. Competing reductions fail: mere wordplay; ignoring the a fortiori; this chapter as already Chapters 62–65; the Son-claim reduced to the judges’ title. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving this as Christ’s reasoning from what is written. The dedicated sense and why of “cannot be broken” remain later because they are later questions. Movement VIII continues. The third verdict of Movement VIII is in force.

The essential architecture is:

> **Citation-file already stated → reasoning from what is written defined → logic defined → weight defined → a fortiori defined → connectives controlled → standing-clause used as force → chain recalled → lesser and greater cases → inference reconstructed → Graphē as court → positive warrant → later interpreter-authority refused → reductions refused → reasoning-file warranted → sequence to “the scripture cannot be broken.”**

The governing distinctions are:

- **Reasoning from what is written** is not **quotation without movement**.
- **Logic of the argument** is not **a heap of clauses**.
- **Weight of the written text** is not **decoration**.
- **A fortiori** is not **identity of the two cases**.
- **Exhibiting the logic** is not **Chapters 62–63**.
- **Court in this dispute** is not **the Chapter 65 gate**.
- **His reasoning** is not **every later interpreter’s Christ-level authority**.
- **Related vocabulary** is not **equivocation**.
- **This file** is not **Chapter 59 retried**, not **Chapter 60 retried**, and not **Chapter 48 retried**.
- **Limits** are **the shape of the doctrine**, not **delayed doubt**.
- **Sequence** is **not hesitation about this level**.

The decisive principle is:

> **Show the logic of Christ’s argument and the weight He assigns to the written text, claiming what that reasoning warrants and not more: He argues a fortiori from the Graphē as court, from the standing naming of those who received God’s word as “gods” to the sanctified and sent Son’s claim, before the finished why of unbreakability, before John 17:17, and before the Graphē-gate. Draw the conclusion the premises support. Do not draw the conclusions that still require later premises. Then ask what it means that the scripture cannot be broken.**

---

# Transition to Chapter 62

Movement VIII continues. Its third word has been stated.

The central witness has been located in history, identified as the Truth, authenticated in claims and works, examined at the hinge of death and raising, attested by positioned seers, shown to confirm the Scriptures He received, shown to send apostles, and shown to authenticate the New Testament witness as continuous with earlier Scripture. The body of writings so treated has been identified, recognized, grounded, exhibited as one testimony, distinguished as to operations, warranted as inspired record, shown not to fail as record, and synthesized as the written Word of the God who cannot lie. That written Word has been heard in a particular controversy: John 10:34–36, the Dedication scene, the blasphemy-charge, the appeal to what is written in their law. The writing so cited has been heard in its own argument: Psalm 82, the judicial address, “I have said, Ye are gods,” those to whom the word of God came. The reasoning from that writing has now been followed: the a fortiori, the court, the weight of the written text as settling-material.

The writings that present that reasoning do not leave unused the further question of the standing-clause that made the lesser case non-negotiable. The logic has been followed. The weight has been shown. A standing-clause still leaves the dedicated account of the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken,” and of what “broken” means in its argumentative context. The next necessary question is therefore not a new curiosity. It is the statement:

> **What is the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken,” now that that clause has been shown to function as the asserted standing of the writing in Christ’s a fortiori from Psalm 82:6, and now that the next file’s first word is to be the statement and the sense of “broken” rather than a second reconstruction of the logic?**

That is the subject of:

# Chapter 62 — “The Scripture Cannot Be Broken”

> **Examine the exact statement and what “broken” means in its argumentative context.**

The investigation now moves from:

> **Christ’s reasoning from what is written**
>
> to:
>
> **the statement that the scripture cannot be broken.**

# End of Chapter 61

title: “The Scripture Cannot Be Broken”
body:
> **Movement VIII — Christ's Verdict on the Graphē**

> **Central objective:** Examine the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken” and what “broken” means in its argumentative context — not as a slogan detached from the a fortiori, not as a second reconstruction of the logic, not as mere rhetoric, not as a claim about manuscript survival only, not as the dedicated “why” from what Scripture is, not as John 17:17, and not as the Graphē-gate. This continues Movement VIII. It is not Chapter 59 retried, not Chapter 60 retried, not Chapter 61 retried, not Chapters 63–65 written in advance, and not a transfer of unbreakability to every later copy, interpreter, or tradition.

---

## Chapter Assignment

Chapter 61 established Movement VIII’s third word. John 10:35–36, read as the dedicated reasoning of the argument already located in Chapter 59 and supplied with its exhibit in Chapter 60, is an a fortiori from what is written. If the writing calls those to whom the word of God came “gods,” and the scripture cannot be broken, then the charge “Thou blasphemest,” spoken of Him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world because He said “I am the Son of God,” is a charge their law will not sustain as a mere inference from God-vocabulary used of a man. He treats the Graphē as the court, not as decoration. He assigns the written text the weight of settling-material for the charge’s terms. The parenthetical “cannot be broken” was used in that file as asserted standing in the chain, not as the finished lexical and doctrinal treatment. The reasoning-file is already in force. Movement VIII continues.

Chapter 61 ended by naming the next necessary question, not a new curiosity:

> **What is the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken,” now that that clause has been shown to function as the asserted standing of the writing in Christ’s a fortiori from Psalm 82:6, and now that the next file’s first word is to be the statement and the sense of “broken” rather than a second reconstruction of the logic?**

That is this chapter’s assignment.

The locked Table of Contents states the work in one sentence:

> **Examine the exact statement and what “broken” means in its argumentative context.**

The locked John 10:34–36 guidance assigns ten steps to the arc as a whole. This chapter is step 7 of that arc: explain “the scripture cannot be broken.” The complete passage has already been located (Chapter 59). The cited writing has already been heard as Psalm 82 (Chapter 60). The logic of the a fortiori and the weight of the written text have already been followed (Chapter 61). The present file examines the exact statement itself: what is said, what λυθῆναι means as the argument uses it, and what cannot be done to the scripture in this dispute. It does not ask why the scripture cannot be broken as the finished why from the doctrine of what Scripture is. It does not connect that why to John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine. It does not conclude that the Graphē is the primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense. Those later steps remain later because they are later questions. Naming them is not performing them.

The chapter does not re-prove that God cannot lie. It cites Chapters 11–12 as established. It does not re-prove γραφή as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ. It cites Chapters 20–22 as established. It does not re-try Christ’s historical place, identity as the Truth, or the claims-and-works conjunction. It cites Chapters 43–45 as established. It does not re-try confirmation of received Scripture as Movement VI’s dedicated file. It cites Chapter 48 as established. It does not re-try corpus, recognition, inspiration, infallibility, or the Movement VII synthesis. It cites Chapters 51–58 as established. It does not re-try the Dedication controversy or the complete passage as a unit. It cites Chapter 59 as established. It does not re-try Psalm 82’s judicial argument, addressees, or the reason the written wording rather than a paraphrase is the exhibit. It cites Chapter 60 as established. It does not re-try the a fortiori, the lesser and greater cases, or the Graphē as court. It cites Chapter 61 as established. It does not treat the dedicated why as concluded. It does not treat John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine. It does not claim that the Graphē is primary written authority in the Movement VIII sense. It performs the examination without which the later why would explain a slogan rather than a statement whose sense in the argument has been controlled.

A standing-clause, now used as force in a reconstructed a fortiori, still leaves a further question. What, exactly, is asserted when He says that the scripture cannot be broken, and what does “broken” mean as that assertion functions in the dispute? Naming neighbourhood is not controlling the statement. The present file is that control, at the level the premises warrant, and not beyond it.

The remaining questions of Movement VIII follow. Sequence continues the investigation. It does not convert the present line into hesitation.

---

## Central Objective

> **To examine, from the biblical record and from premises already in force, the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken” and what “broken” means in its argumentative context, so that Movement VIII’s fourth word is one inspectable conclusion: the statement is Christ’s assertion of the Graphē’s standing in the court He has opened; “broken,” as λυθῆναι functions in this dispute, is not a slogan, not a claim about manuscript survival only, and not yet the dedicated why; it names what cannot be done to the writing here — the writing’s force cannot be set aside, loosed, annulled, or made void so as to evacuate His appeal; to keep that examination distinct from Chapter 63’s why from what Scripture is, from John 17:17, and from the Graphē-gate; to refuse the reduction of the statement to mere rhetoric, the reduction of it to textual transmission only, and the collapse of this file into Chapters 63–65; and to refuse both under-claim and over-claim.**

The governing movement is:

> **Movement VIII’s third word already stated → question of the exact statement and of “broken” → the statement defined → “broken” defined for this argument → English rendering distinguished from Greek range → lexical control of λύω / λυθῆναι → grammatical control of οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή → neighbouring Johannine and Synoptic uses illuminating range without capture → what cannot be done to the scripture in this dispute → the clause in its place in the unit → assertion of standing in the opened court, not a slogan detached from the a fortiori → force cannot be set aside or made void so as to evacuate the appeal → “cannot” as asserted incapacity of the writing → ἡ γραφή as subject → parenthetical as non-optional → what setting aside would do to the a fortiori → positive warrant → their law as the writing they may not break → competing reductions refused → inspectable inference → warranted conclusion → sequence to why the scripture cannot be broken.**

The chapter’s conclusion is affirmative:

> **John 10:35b, read as the dedicated examination of the exact statement already located in Chapter 59 and already used as force in Chapter 61’s a fortiori, is Christ’s assertion of the Graphē’s standing in the court He has opened. “The scripture cannot be broken” is not a flourish beside the citation. It is not a claim that every later copy is physically indestructible. It is the assertion that ἡ γραφή cannot be λυθῆναι: the writing cannot be loosed, undone, annulled, or set aside so as to make the written lesser case disposable and the appeal empty. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in treating this as the sense of the statement in its argumentative context, step 7 of the locked John 10 arc. It is not yet Chapter 63’s why from what Scripture is. It is not yet John 17:17. It is not yet the Graphē-gate. It is the exact statement, controlled. Movement VIII continues. That is this chapter’s conclusion, stated here with full force.**

The remaining questions follow by sequence. The statement is already in force as controlled sense, not as postponed guesswork.

---

# 62.1 The Question Created by the Preceding Chapter

Movement VIII has opened and continued. John 10:34–36 has been examined as a complete argument in the Dedication controversy: an appeal to what is written as decisive in a dispute over blasphemy. Psalm 82 has been examined as the cited writing’s own argument: a judicial psalm whose verse 6 addresses as gods those who judge under God, those to whom the word of God came, used as written wording rather than as a paraphrase. The reasoning from that wording has been followed: if the writing so names them, and the scripture cannot be broken, the charge of blasphemy against the Father’s sanctified and sent Son, because He said “I am the Son of God,” is a charge the writing will not sustain. The Graphē has been shown as court, not decoration. The standing-clause has been used as force in that chain. It has not yet been examined, as this movement’s dedicated file, as the exact statement it is, or as to what “broken” means in that argumentative setting.

Chapter 61 established the reasoning-file. That conclusion is a premise here. A reconstructed a fortiori still leaves a further question: if the lesser naming forces the greater application only because the writing is treated as unbreakable standing, what is that unbreakability as the argument states it, and what act is being denied when He says the scripture cannot be broken? Using a clause as force names the function. The present file examines the statement.

A people can receive the Dedication scene as a controversy, receive verses 34–36 as an answer, receive Psalm 82 as the psalm, receive the a fortiori as logic, and still leave unasked what the exact words “the scripture cannot be broken” assert, and what “broken” does in the dispute. The writings themselves force the further analysis. He says οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή. That sentence, already in the unit, already used as force, has a sense. If it has none that can be controlled, “the scripture cannot be broken” is a title. If it has every consequence a later slogan wishes, the investigation has stopped examining the statement.

The question is therefore not:

> **How does Christ reason from the written wording of Psalm 82:6 to the present charge, and what weight does He assign to the written text in that reasoning?**

That question has been answered.

The question is:

> **What is the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken,” and what does “broken” mean in the argumentative context in which He asserts it?**

If Movement VIII proceeded from the a fortiori to the dedicated why without controlling the statement, it would explain a slogan. If it treated this file as already Chapter 63, it would consume the later why from what Scripture is before the statement’s sense has been examined. If it treated this file as already Chapters 64–65, it would consume Word-as-truth and the Graphē-gate before “broken” has been controlled. If it treated this file as a retry of Chapter 59, it would convert a statement-file into a second scene-description. If it treated this file as a retry of Chapter 61, it would convert a statement-file into a second logic-file. The present file is the dedicated examination of the exact statement and of “broken.”

That is a different operation from piety. It is the operation this chapter must perform.

---

# 62.2 What This Chapter Does Not Repeat

Chapters 1–3 established truth as conformity to reality, distinct from belief, popularity, and institutional consensus. Chapters 4–7 established knowledge, evidence, reason, and rational warrant as inspectable operations. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-write the opening epistemology. It uses reason as already defined, now as the standard against which the exact statement is examined as an assertion in an argument, not as a pious noise.

Chapters 10–12 established that God is the ground of truth, that He is truthful, faithful, and immutable, and that falsehood is incompatible with Him. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-write the impossibility of divine falsehood. It does not convert those premises into Chapter 63’s dedicated why. It uses them as already in force for any later claim that the writing of which this statement is made is God’s writing.

Chapters 20–22 established γραφή (*graphē*, G1124) as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ / Scripture. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the lexical file of γραφή. It uses the term as John 10:35 uses it: ἡ γραφή, the subject of which “cannot be broken” is said.

Chapter 40 established manuscripts, transmission, and preservation as the historical question of how the written record has been copied and kept. That conclusion remains a premise for a distinction this chapter must draw. This chapter does not re-try the transmission-file. It refuses, later, the reduction of John 10:35b to that file under another name.

Chapters 43–45 established Jesus Christ as a corroborated historical figure, identified in the authentic testimony as the Truth and the revealer of the Father, and authenticated in claims and works. Chapter 48 established His confirmation of the Scriptures He received as binding written word, including Matthew 5:17–18’s refusal to destroy the Law and the Prophets. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try existence, identity, works as witness, or confirmation as a general practice. It uses neighbouring λύω-family uses as illumination, not as a second confirmation-file.

Chapters 51–58 established corpus, recognition, prophetic-apostolic ground, unity of testimony, distinction of operations, inspiration’s guarantees, infallibility of the record, and the synthesis of truth, authority, and the written Word. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try Movement VII. It uses the Graphē’s standing as written Word as already-cleared ground for identifying what ἡ γραφή names, without converting that standing into the dedicated why of unbreakability.

Chapter 59 established the complete passage, the Dedication controversy, the blasphemy-charge, the appeal to what is written, the naming of Psalm 82:6, the characterization “unto whom the word of God came,” the presence of “cannot be broken” in the unit, and the application to the sanctified and sent Son. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the Dedication scene, winter, Solomon’s porch, or the three-verse unit as a first locating.

Chapter 60 established the actual citation as Psalm 82:6 in the psalm’s judicial argument, the addressees as those who judge under God and received His word, and the reason He uses the written wording rather than a paraphrase. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-give the psalm verse by verse.

Chapter 61 established the a fortiori, the Graphē as court, the weight of the written text as settling-material, and the use of “cannot be broken” as force in the chain. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the lesser and greater cases, the reconstruction of the inference, or the distinction between His reasoning and later interpreters’ authority. It uses that chain in order to control the statement that made the lesser case non-negotiable.

This chapter does not recatalogue Matthew 4 and Luke 24 as if confirmation were still in doubt. It does not treat 2 Timothy 3:15–17 as a second inspiration-file. It does not invent unverifiable details of a particular scroll in the porch, a reconstructed academy, or a later scholarly quarrel as the chapter’s center. The new function is this:

> **To examine the exact statement “the scripture cannot be broken” and what “broken” means in its argumentative context; to refuse both emptiness and overclaim; and to leave the dedicated why, John 17:17, and the Graphē-gate in their assigned files.**

---

# 62.3 Define the Question: The Exact Statement and “Broken”

**The exact statement**, in this chapter, is the clause Christ asserts in John 10:35:

> **“…and the scripture cannot be broken…”**

In the received Greek of the verse the clause is:

> **…καὶ οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή…**

The statement is easily abused. In ordinary speech “the scripture cannot be broken” may mean a preacher’s motto, a claim that no manuscript can perish, a boast that every later tradition is thereby certified, a psychological remark that opponents will fail to refute a text, or a claim that Chapters 63–65 are already finished because a clause exists. None of those senses is this chapter’s object.

Four elements belong to the definition.

First, **the exact statement**. The object is the clause as spoken in the unit, not a later expansion, not a poster-fragment, and not a chain of neighbouring verses offered as substitutes for this sentence. Neighbouring uses of λύω will illuminate range. They will not replace the statement.

Second, **“broken” in its argumentative context**. The object is what λυθῆναι names as the argument uses it in this dispute: what cannot be done to the scripture here, such that the written lesser case remains standing and the appeal is not evacuated. Context is the Dedication blasphemy-trial already located, the citation already heard, the a fortiori already followed. Context is not a license to invent a setting the record does not give.

Third, **as Christ’s assertion of the Graphē’s standing in the court He has opened**. The statement is not a later church’s slogan attached to His name. It is His assertion, in the dispute, about ἡ γραφή. Standing, in this chapter, is the writing’s force as court-material that may not be loosed. Standing so defined is not yet the dedicated why, and it is not yet the Graphē-gate.

Fourth, **not those other claims**. The definition excludes, as not this object: the dedicated why from what Scripture is; John 17:17 as finished Graphē-doctrine; the Graphē-gate; a retry of Chapter 59’s scene; a retry of Chapter 60’s psalm; a retry of Chapter 61’s logic as if the statement had no remaining sense to examine; a claim that every later copy is physically unbreakable; a grant that every later interpreter’s use of a verse inherits this standing. Those exclusions are part of the definition. They are not a later apology.

Thus:

> **The question of this chapter is not whether John 10:34–36 is an argument from writing, what Psalm 82 argues, how the a fortiori is drawn, or why Scripture cannot be broken as a finished doctrine from what Scripture is. Those questions have been examined or remain later. The question is what the exact statement asserts, and what “broken” means in the argument in which He asserts it.**

---

# 62.4 Distinguish Eight Objects That Must Not Be Collapsed

The investigation fails at the first step if it treats different objects as one.

## 62.4.1 Examining the statement and Chapter 63’s dedicated why

This chapter controls what the statement means in the argument. Chapter 63 will answer why the scripture cannot be broken from what Scripture is: authoritative written truth, not merely from the fact that Jesus quoted the clause. Sense is not why. To treat this file as already Chapter 63 would steal the later ground. To omit the sense in order to protect the later why would leave the why explaining an uncontrolled slogan. The sense is controlled here. The why remains later.

## 62.4.2 Examining the statement and John 17:17

John 17:17 will identify the Father’s word as truth: “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” That identification is Chapter 64’s object. The present statement is about ἡ γραφή and λυθῆναι in a blasphemy-dispute. Neighbourhood in Movement VIII is not identity of files. Word-as-truth is not yet this clause’s sense.

## 62.4.3 This chapter and the Chapter 65 gate

This chapter establishes that in this dispute He asserts that the writing cannot be set aside as court-force. Chapter 65 will conclude that the Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived. Unbreakable standing in one controversy is not the finished gate.

## 62.4.4 This chapter and Chapter 61’s reasoning-file

Chapter 61 used the clause as force in the a fortiori. This chapter examines the clause as statement and controls “broken.” Using a clause and examining a clause are related operations. They are not the same file. Collapse of the two would hide the sense inside a second reconstruction of lesser and greater cases.

## 62.4.5 Argumentative sense and mere rhetoric

Rhetoric, in the competing reduction, is ornamental speech that adds emphasis without adding a claim. The statement adds a claim: ἡ γραφή cannot be λυθῆναι. A flourish does not occupy the joint between characterization and application. The distinction is part of the object. Treating the clause as volume is a competing reduction, not a definition of the object.

## 62.4.6 Argumentative sense and textual transmission only

Chapter 40 examined copying, witnesses, and preservation. Physical survival of copies is a historical question. John 10:35b is a claim about the writing’s force in a dispute. A writing whose copies have been preserved may still be treated as void in argument. A writing treated as unbreakable standing in argument is not thereby a lecture on palaeography. Collapse of the two would convert Movement VIII’s statement-file into a second transmission-file.

## 62.4.7 This chapter and Chapter 59’s Dedication-file

Chapter 59 located the argument and named the clause as belonging to the unit. This chapter examines the named clause. Neighbourhood is not identity. The scene remains premise. The statement is the new object. Collapse of the two would hide λυθῆναι inside a second description of stones and porch.

## 62.4.8 Sense of “broken” and every later use of a verse as unbreakable in the interpreter’s mouth

He asserts that the scripture cannot be broken. Later readers also quote verses. The second fact does not confer the first Person’s assertion upon every later quotation. A later interpreter may cite Scripture validly or may break it in the argumentative sense — set it aside, evacuate it, make it void — even while pronouncing the English words “the scripture cannot be broken.” This distinction is part of the object. Collapse of the two would make Movement IX impossible before it begins.

Thus:

> **The exact statement and the sense of “broken” are this chapter’s object. They are not the dedicated why, not John 17:17, not the Graphē-gate, not Chapter 61 retried, not mere rhetoric, not transmission only, not Chapter 59 retried, and not a grant that every later quotation inherits this standing.**

# 62.6 The Sequence of Levels: One Clean Scope Section

What this chapter does not settle is a matter of sequence, not of doubt about what it does settle.

The investigation proceeds by levels. Each level answers its question with full force. The next level remains next because it is a different question.

**Already in force.** God cannot lie. Revelation has been given and authenticated. Scripture as writing is God-breathed. The warrant is full at this level. It is not postponed until Chapter 63 in order to keep the present sense weak.

The statement is not a grant that every later quotation inherits this standing. Using Chapters 59–61 is not rewriting them. Those limits are part of what the statement-file is. They are not a stack of clauses designed to drain the positive conclusion.

# 62.7 The Exact Statement Defined

**The exact statement**, controlled as wording rather than as a later expansion, is this:

> **“the scripture cannot be broken.”**

The statement has a subject, a modal verb of incapacity, and an infinitive of the act denied.

The **subject** is ἡ γραφή — the scripture, the writing already named in biblical usage as Holy Writ. In this argument the writing is the cited Scripture: the wording of Psalm 82:6 treated as written in their law, characterized as a calling of those to whom the word of God came. The subject is not the interpreter. The subject is not a later English volume as object. The subject is the writing.

The **incapacity** is οὐ δύναται — is not able. δύναμαι (*dynamai*, G1410) is to be able, to have power. With οὐ the clause denies ability. The denial is predicated of the writing: the scripture is not able to be subjected to the act named by the infinitive. The grammar is not first a command to the opponents, though it bars what they would have to do to sustain the charge. It is first an assertion about the writing.

The **act denied** is λυθῆναι — to be loosed, undone, broken, in the sense the next sections will control. The infinitive is aorist passive. The writing is the patient of the denied act.

The **conjunction** is καί — “and.” Chapter 61 already located this καί as joining the standing-clause to the condition as a parenthetical of force inside the sentence that reaches verse 36’s application. This chapter uses that location: the statement is not a new discourse. It is the asserted character of the writing being used as case.

The exact statement is therefore not three English words chosen for a motto. It is a Greek clause with inspectable joints, spoken as part of an argument already reconstructed. A motto can be moved to any controversy. This clause occupies this controversy: between “unto whom the word of God came” and “Say ye of him… Thou blasphemest.”

Two false substitutes must be refused at the definition.

**The statement as a later creed-sentence.** Later theology may formulate “Scripture is unbreakable.” Formulation may be accurate or inaccurate. The present object is His clause in His argument. The later creed-sentence, if it is true, will have to answer to this clause. It does not replace this clause.

**The statement as a heap of neighbouring verses.** Psalm 119, Proverbs 30:5–6, Isaiah 40:8, Matthew 5:18, and 1 Peter 1:25 are writings that bear upon the standing of God’s word. They are not this statement. Neighbouring illumination will be used as illumination. Substitution of a heap for the clause would be the proof-texting the methodology forbids.

Thus:

> **The exact statement is οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή, asserted of the writing in the argument of John 10:35–36. Subject, incapacity, and denied act are the joints. A motto and a heap are not the statement.**

# 62.8 “Broken” Defined for This Argument

**“Broken,”** in this chapter, is the English rendering of λυθῆναι in John 10:35, controlled by lexical range, grammatical form, Johannine and related biblical usage, and — decisively — the argumentative context of the Dedication blasphemy-dispute.

The definition for this argument is this:

> **To “break” the scripture here is to loose it, undo it, dissolve its force, annul it, or set it aside as court-material, so that the written case no longer stands as binding premise and the appeal from that case is evacuated.**

What cannot be done, therefore, is that act. The scripture cannot be treated as a disposable illustration, a dead relic, an optional colour around stones, or a wording that may be voided in order to keep the charge alive.

Four elements belong to this definition.

First, **an act upon the writing**. λυθῆναι is something that would be done to ἡ γραφή. The statement is not first a remark about the opponents’ feelings, the crowd’s noise, or the physical weather of the porch. It is about the writing.

Second, **force, not mere physical fracture as the governing image**. English “broken” easily suggests a snapped object. Greek λύω easily includes loosing what was bound, dissolving what stood, annulling what was in force. In a dispute whose first word is “Is it not written in your law,” the governing image is the loosing of a written standing, not the snapping of a scroll as artefact.

Third, **so as to evacuate the appeal**. The sense is not an abstract property floating free of verses 34–36. It is the sense required by the a fortiori already followed: if the lesser naming may be loosed at will, it cannot force the application in verse 36. The statement denies that loosing.

Fourth, **not the dedicated why**. The definition says what cannot be done. It does not, as this file’s achievement, say why the writing has that character from the doctrine of what Scripture is. Why remains Chapter 63. Defining the act denied is not answering that why.

Two further English traps must be named and refused.

**“Broken” as “incorrect.”** Modern English may say a statement is “broken” meaning faulty, failed, or untrue. That is not this clause. He does not say the scripture cannot be false as a later inerrancy-slogan detached from the dispute, though Movement VII has already warranted the record’s truthfulness as writing. He says the scripture cannot be λυθῆναι. The argumentative force is standing that cannot be loosed, not a modern idiom of malfunction.

**“Broken” as “sadly unheeded.”** A later piety may hear “cannot be broken” as “ought not to be ignored.” Ought is not cannot. The clause is οὐ δύναται, not οὐ δεῖ. He asserts incapacity of the writing to be so treated, not merely a moral preference that it not be so treated. Preference would not make the lesser case non-negotiable. Incapacity of the writing to be loosed does.

Thus:

> **“Broken” in this argument is the loosing, undoing, annulling, or setting aside of the writing’s force as court, such that the appeal would be evacuated. It is not a snapped artefact as the governing sense, not “incorrect,” and not a mere “ought.”**

---

# 62.9 English “Broken” and Greek λύω Distinguished

The investigation must not let an English word silently govern a Greek clause.

**Broken**, in English, commonly names fracture: a bone, a seal, a contract, a law, a promise. The legal uses — broken law, broken covenant — already approach the argumentative sense. The physical uses — broken jar, broken scroll — do not. A translation is not a crime. A translation that is then read only as physics becomes a capture.

**λύω (*lyō*, G3089)** has a range the next section will exhibit: to loose what is bound; to unbind; to set free; to undo; to dissolve; to destroy; to break up; to repeal or violate a commandment or a standing ordinance. The English “broken” in John 10:35 is one rendering of that range in the passive. It is not the whole range, and it is not a license to pick the most convenient English picture.

The methodological rule already in force is:

> **Original script → transliteration → lexical form → Strong’s number where relevant → basic lexical meaning → grammatical form → biblical usage → contextual meaning → argumentative significance.**

Lexical meaning is not yet contextual meaning. Contextual meaning is not yet a later theological slogan. The present file will walk that sequence for λυθῆναι and then return to the dispute as the control.

Honesty about rendering requires a further distinction. Other English versions may say “cannot be annulled,” “cannot be set aside,” “cannot be undone.” Those renderings are not rival scriptures. They are attempts to name the same Greek infinitive. This chapter does not select a commercial version as authority. It uses the received English “cannot be broken” as the locked title’s wording, and it controls that wording by the Greek and by the argument. Where “annulled” or “set aside” illuminates the argumentative sense, those English words are used as exposition, not as a replacement canon.

Thus:

> **English “broken” is the received rendering. Greek λύω is the verb. The argument, not a physical picture of fracture, controls which stretch of the range is in force here.**

---

# 62.10 Lexical Control of λύω (G3089)

The preferred lexical sequence may now be performed for the verb of the statement.

**Original script.** λύω

**Transliteration.** *lyō*

**Lexical form.** Present active infinitive stem as the lemma; the form in John 10:35 is λυθῆναι.

**Strong’s.** G3089.

**Basic lexical meaning.** To loose; to unbind; to undo; to dissolve; to destroy; to break up; to set free; by extension, to repeal, violate, or annul what stands as bound — a commandment, an ordinance, a law.

**Grammatical form in John 10:35.** λυθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive. Aorist names the act as such, not a colourless present process. Passive names the writing as the patient of the act. Infinitive, under οὐ δύναται, names the act as that of which the writing is not capable of being the patient.

**Biblical usage**, sampled as range, not as a catalogue offered in place of John 10.

The verb looses what is bound in ordinary action: sandals (Mark 1:7); an animal on the Sabbath (Luke 13:15); Lazarus’s graveclothes (John 11:44). Those uses establish the root image: what was fastened is unfastened.

The verb destroys or dissolves what stood as a structure: “Destroy this temple” — λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον (John 2:19); the middle wall of partition (Ephesians 2:14); the works of the devil (1 John 3:8); the heavens and elements in 2 Peter 3:10–12. Those uses establish that λύω can name demolition.

The verb looses in the legal and ordinance-sense that will prove nearest this dispute. John 5:18: He “had broken the sabbath” — ἔλυεν τὸ σάββατον. John 7:23: circumcision on the Sabbath is performed “that the law of Moses should not be broken” — ἵνα μὴ λυθῇ ὁ νόμος Μωϋσέως. Matthew 5:19: “whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments” — ὃς ἐὰν οὖν λύσῃ μίαν τῶν ἐντολῶν τούτων τῶν ἐλαχίστων. The related compound καταλύω in Matthew 5:17 names destroying or abolishing the Law and the Prophets. Those uses establish that written or standing ordinance can be the object of λύω: to break a commandment is to loose its force as binding, to treat it as not standing.

**Contextual meaning in John 10:35.** The object is ἡ γραφή. The setting is “your law.” The function is the standing of a written case used to try a capital charge. The nearest stretch of the range is therefore the ordinance-sense: to loose, annul, or set aside the writing as binding court-material. Demolition of a building is in the range and is not the governing picture here. Unbinding a sandal is in the range and is not the governing picture here. The sandal-uses teach the root. The law-uses teach the application.

**Argumentative significance.** If ἡ γραφή could be λυθῆναι in this sense, Psalm 82:6 could be treated as not standing, and verse 36 would have no written premise that must be answered. The statement denies that possibility as a possibility about the writing.

Lexical control illuminates. It does not replace the argument. A lexicon cannot, by itself, finish Chapter 63, and it cannot, by itself, convert this file into John 17:17.

Thus:

> **λύω ranges from loosing what is bound to dissolving what stands, including the annulling of commandment and law. In John 10:35 the contextual stretch is that ordinance-sense applied to ἡ γραφή: the writing cannot be loosed as standing court.**

---

# 62.11 Grammatical Control: οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή

Grammar is not a later system imposed upon piety. It is the statement’s own joints.

**ἡ γραφή.** Nominative singular, articular. The writing is the subject of δύναται. Chapters 20–22 already established the term. This chapter needs the grammatical fact: what “cannot” is said of is the scripture, not first the opponents, not first the stones, not first a later copyist.

**οὐ δύναται.** Third person singular present: is not able. The present of δύναται with this infinitive asserts a standing incapacity, not a momentary mood. He does not say that on this winter day, in this porch, the writing happens to be unbroken. He says it cannot be broken.

**λυθῆναι.** Aorist passive infinitive completing δύναται. The construction “is not able to be λυθῆναι” names an impossibility of the writing’s being subjected to that act. The aorist does not require a reconstructed timeline of a future snapping. It names the act as such.

**καί.** The clause is joined, not isolated. Grammar agrees with argument: parenthetical of force inside the sentence, not a new title.

What the grammar forbids is as important as what it states.

It forbids hearing the clause as first a psychological report: “they will not succeed in breaking it,” as if the subject were the opponents’ competence. The subject is ἡ γραφή.

It forbids hearing the clause as first a command: “do not break it,” as if the mood were imperative. The mood is indicative of incapacity.

It forbids hearing the clause as first a wish: “may it not be broken.” He asserts.

It does not, by itself, finish the why. Grammar can say that incapacity is asserted of the writing. Grammar cannot, in this file, consume Chapter 63’s account of that incapacity from what Scripture is.

Thus:

> **The grammar of John 10:35b asserts, in the indicative, that the writing is not able to be subjected to λυθῆναι. The subject is ἡ γραφή. The mood is not imperative, not optative, and not a report of the opponents’ skill.**

---

# 62.12 Neighbouring Johannine Uses: John 7:23 and John 5:18

The Fourth Gospel uses λύω of standing ordinance before it uses λυθῆναι of ἡ γραφή. Those uses are illumination. They are not a second Dedication-scene, and they are not this statement under another name.

## 62.12.1 John 7:23 — that the law of Moses should not be broken

> **“If a man on the sabbath day receive circumcision, that the law of Moses should not be broken; are ye angry at me, because I have made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day?”**
> — John 7:23

The purpose clause is ἵνα μὴ λυθῇ ὁ νόμος Μωϋσέως. λυθῇ is aorist passive subjunctive of the same verb. The object is the law of Moses. Circumcision on the eighth day, even when that day is a Sabbath, is performed so that Moses’ law not be loosed. The argument is a fortiori of a different controversy: if the law’s standing requires a Sabbath circumcision, how much more a Sabbath making-whole. The present file does not retry that controversy as Chapter 45’s works-file or as a finished Sabbath-doctrine.

What the verse contributes here is lexical and forensic control. In John’s Gospel, λύω in the passive, with law as subject-patient, names the loosing of written standing. “Broken” in that sentence is not the snapping of a scroll. It is the treating of Moses’ law as not in force at the point where it commands. That is the nearest Johannine neighbour to οὐ δύναται λυθῆναι ἡ γραφή.

The neighbour is not identity. John 7:23 concerns ὁ νόμος Μωϋσέως in a Sabbath-healing dispute. John 10:35 concerns ἡ γραφή in a blasphemy-dispute, with a psalm called written in their law. Law and scripture are related in the discourse; they are not collapsed into one lemma. The contribution is the sense of λυθῆναι when a standing writing is the patient: to be loosed as binding.

## 62.12.2 John 5:18 — he had broken the sabbath

> **“…because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God.”**
> — John 5:18

ἔλυεν τὸ σάββατον. The imperfect active names what the opponents charge: He was loosing the Sabbath. Chapter 45 already used this verse as the height of the claim in the works-argument. This chapter takes only the verb. “Broken the sabbath,” in the narrator’s report of their charge, is violation or loosing of a standing ordinance, not demolition of a day as an astronomical object.

The contribution is again range under control. The same Gospel can use λύω of loosing Sabbath-standing. When the same Gospel later says the scripture cannot be λυθῆναι, it is not inventing a nonce-verb. It is applying, to ἡ γραφή, the ordinance-sense already in Johannine usage.

The neighbour is not a claim that John 10 is only a Sabbath-text. It is not a retry of equality-with-God as Chapter 45. It is the verb’s Johannine forensic use.

Thus:

> **John 7:23 and John 5:18 show λύω, in this Gospel, loosing standing ordinance — the law of Moses, the Sabbath. That stretch of the range illuminates John 10:35 without absorbing it. “Broken” as loosed standing is Johannine before it is said of ἡ γραφή.**

---

# 62.13 Neighbouring Synoptic Uses: Matthew 5:17–19, Used Not Retried

Chapter 48 already established Matthew 5:17–18 as confirmation: He has not come to destroy the Law or the Prophets; jot and tittle will not pass until all be fulfilled. That conclusion remains a premise. This chapter does not rewrite the Sermon as a confirmation-file. It takes the λύω-family in the neighbouring verse.

Matthew 5:17 uses the compound **καταλῦσαι (*katalusai*, from καταλύω, G2647)**: to loosen down, demolish, abolish. “Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets.” Destruction there is abolition of the received writings as standing. He refuses that role.

Matthew 5:19 uses λύω itself:

> **“Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”**

λύσῃ is aorist active subjunctive: whoever shall break, shall loose, one of the least commandments. Breaking a commandment, in that sentence, is not snapping a tablet. It is loosing a commandment’s force while teaching others to treat it as loosed. Doing and teaching is the opposite: treating the commandment as standing.

The contribution to John 10:35 is controlled and limited.

The Synoptic neighbour shows that the λύω-family, in Christ’s own speech about written commandment, names loosing of standing, not physical fracture as the governing sense.

The neighbour shows that “least commandments” can be the object. John 10:35’s object is ἡ γραφή as the writing whose wording is the case. A commandment loosed and a scripture loosed are analogous operations upon standing writing. Analogy is not identity of files.

The neighbour must not be used to steal Chapter 63. Matthew 5:18’s jot and tittle, already used in Chapter 48, bear upon why written marks are not treated as disposable. That bearing is confirmation-stage. The dedicated why of John 10:35 from what Scripture is remains later. Illumination is not consumption.

Thus:

> **Matthew 5:17–19, already in force as confirmation, illuminates λύω as loosing of commandment and καταλύω as abolition of Law and Prophets. That illumination serves the sense of John 10:35. It does not retry Chapter 48, and it does not finish Chapter 63.**
